questions.q: What is bookkeeping?
options: The system used to record a firm's financial transactions — a routine, clerical process
questions.explain: Accounting goes further: interpreting and reporting the recorded data.
questions.evidence: Bookkeeping, the system used to record a firm’s financial transactions, is a routine, clerical process.

questions.q: What are liabilities?
options: What a firm owes to its creditors
questions.explain: Liabilities are also called debts.
questions.evidence: Liabilities—also called debts —are what a firm owes to its creditors.

questions.q: What is depreciation?
options: Allocating an asset's original cost to the years in which it is expected to produce revenues
A fall in the company's share price
questions.explain: It matches the cost of long-lived assets to the revenue they help earn.
questions.evidence: Depreciation is the allocation of the asset’s original cost to the years in which it is expected to produce revenues.

questions.q: Why is gross profit a critical number?
options: It is the amount paid in tax
It is the source of funds to cover all the firm's other expenses
It shows cash in the bank
questions.explain: Gross profit = net sales − cost of goods sold.
questions.evidence: Gross profit is a critical number for a company because it is the source of funds to cover all the firm’s other expenses.

questions.q: What does the acid-test (quick) ratio measure?
options: A firm's ability to pay its current liabilities without selling inventory
The share of debt in total financing
questions.explain: It excludes inventory, the least liquid current asset.
questions.evidence: The acid-test ratio is used to measure the firm’s ability to pay its current liabilities without selling inventory.

questions.q: Why must low-margin businesses be 'high volume'?
options: Because their prices are set by government
Because they must sell a lot of product to be profitable
questions.explain: Margin is the selling price minus the unit cost.
questions.evidence: Low margin businesses must be “high volume,” meaning they must sell a lot of product to be profitable.

questions.q: What is the 'Ten Point Test'?
options: Ten key ratios that together summarise a government's liquidity, profitability and solvency
A test of ten budget assumptions
questions.explain: Comparing ratios with peers shows relative financial health.
questions.evidence: It’s comprised of ten key ratios that, when taken together, summarize a government’s liquidity, profitability, and solvency.

questions.q: What is financial management?
options: Only the work of the accounting department
The art and science of managing a firm's money so that it can meet its goals
questions.explain: It is not just the responsibility of the finance department.
questions.evidence: Financial management—the art and science of managing a firm’s money so that it can meet its goals—is not just the responsibility of the finance department.

questions.q: What is cash management?
options: Counting the cash in the till each night
Making sure enough cash is on hand to pay bills as they come due and to meet unexpected expenses
questions.explain: Temporary surpluses can be invested in marketable securities.
questions.evidence: An important duty of the financial manager is cash management, or making sure that enough cash is on hand to pay bills as they come due and to meet unexpected expenses.

questions.q: What is the primary market?
options: Where used securities are traded between investors
Where new securities are sold to the public, usually with the help of investment bankers
questions.explain: Existing securities then trade in the secondary market.
questions.evidence: The primary market is where new securities are sold to the public, usually with the help of investment bankers.

questions.q: What does the book say about using one-time revenues?
options: They should never be used to fund the operating budget
questions.explain: Recurring costs need recurring revenues.
questions.evidence: This is why one-time revenues should never be used to fund the operating budget.

questions.q: What is one of the main goals of full cost accounting?
options: Removing indirect costs from the books
Distributing indirect costs to cost centres
questions.explain: Full cost reveals what each service really costs, including overheads.
questions.evidence: One of the main goals of full cost accounting is to distribute indirect costs to cost centers.

questions.q: How does the chapter describe accounting's role in a business?
options: The backbone of the business, giving a framework to understand its financial condition
A legal formality with little practical use
questions.explain: Managers use accounting information to make decisions.
questions.evidence: accounting is the backbone of any business, providing a framework to understand the firm’s financial condition

questions.q: Who benefits from knowing the basics of accounting and financial statements?
options: All of us, whatever our work situation
questions.explain: Employees, owners, investors and even people outside the workforce all use financial information.
questions.evidence: benefit from knowing the basics of accounting and financial statements

questions.q: Which questions does financial statement analysis help answer about an organisation?
options: Do its staff like their jobs?
Is it liquid, profitable and solvent?
questions.explain: It also compares the organisation with its peers.
questions.evidence: Is it liquid? Profitable? Solvent?

questions.q: In the landslide story, why did two financially stressed fire districts send personnel?
options: Because the state financial management office called them
questions.explain: Knowing which districts were under financial stress helped save lives.
questions.evidence: had OFM not called, they would not have sent their personnel

questions.q: What is margin (profit margin)?
options: The selling price minus the unit cost
questions.explain: Low-margin businesses need high volume to be profitable.
questions.evidence: Margin (sometimes called the profit margin) is the price at which a good or service is sold, minus the unit cost.

questions.q: Why are profitability measures less important for governments?
options: Governments need not be profitable to keep operating
questions.explain: Liquidity and solvency still matter a great deal.
questions.evidence: Profitability measures are less salient for governments because governments need not be profitable to continue operating.

questions.q: What does a non-profit's program expense ratio show?
options: How fast it pays its bills
How much of its spending goes to programs rather than overhead
questions.explain: Overhead includes administration and fundraising.
questions.evidence: total expenses are invested in its programs and services, rather than administration, fundraising, and other overhead spending

questions.q: Around which three dimensions is financial position analysed?
questions.explain: Different patterns of strength and weakness call for different strategies.
questions.evidence: It is organized around liquidity, profitability, and solvency.

questions.q: A non-profit is profitable and solvent but short of liquidity. What is its challenge?
options: Turning some of its profitability into a stronger base of liquid resources
Taking on as much debt as possible
questions.explain: It may accept slightly weaker solvency as a trade-off.
questions.evidence: Here the challenge is to convert some of that profitability into a stronger base of liquid resources.

questions.q: If long-term liabilities cause solvency concerns, what could an organisation consider?
options: Paying them all off with payroll money
questions.explain: Changing loan terms can ease long-term pressure.
questions.evidence: If long-term liabilities are part of the solvency concern it could consider restructuring or re-negotiating those liabilities.

questions.q: What might an organisation with concerns about liquidity, profitability and solvency consider?
options: More drastic measures, such as merging with another non-profit
questions.explain: Weakness on all three fronts threatens survival.
questions.evidence: organizations with concerns about all three aspects of financial position might consider more drastic measures like a merger with another non-profit

questions.q: What might a non-profit ask donors for to strengthen its liquidity?
questions.explain: Reserves cushion short-term cash shortfalls.
questions.evidence: It might also make a specific ask to donors for a reserve fund or other financial contingency fund to bolster its liquidity.

questions.q: Why do many big companies use commercial paper instead of short-term bank loans?
options: Its interest rate is usually 1–3 percent below bank rates
It never has to be repaid
Banks refuse to lend to big companies
It is guaranteed by the government
questions.explain: Commercial paper is unsecured short-term debt.
questions.evidence: the interest rate on commercial paper is usually 1 to 3 percent below bank rates

questions.q: Where does short-term financing appear on the balance sheet?
questions.explain: It finances current assets and day-to-day operations.
questions.evidence: Short-term financing is shown as a current liability on the balance sheet and is used to finance current assets and support operations.

questions.q: Who are the main sources of secured short-term loans to business?
options: Commercial banks and commercial finance companies
questions.explain: Secured loans are backed by collateral such as inventory or receivables.
questions.evidence: Commercial banks and commercial finance companies are the main sources of secured short-term loans to business.

questions.q: What is a company's first sale of stock to the public called?
questions.explain: After it, the company is closely watched by regulators and analysts.
questions.evidence: first sale of stock to the public is called an initial public offering

questions.q: How does a preferred stock dividend differ from a common stock dividend?
options: It is usually set when the stock is issued
It is always higher than any bond interest
questions.explain: Common stock dividends depend on the board's decisions.
questions.evidence: Unlike common stock, preferred stock usually has a dividend amount that is set at the time the stock is issued.

questions.q: Why is preferred stock more expensive than debt financing?
options: It must be repaid within a year
It gives buyers control of the company
questions.explain: Interest on debt is tax-deductible, which lowers its effective cost.
questions.evidence: Preferred stock is more expensive than debt financing, however, because preferred dividends are not tax-deductible.

questions.q: What is the central point of the budget strategy chapter?
options: How a budget is made matters as much as the revenues and spending in it
Budgets should be made by one person
questions.explain: Process shapes conflict, engagement and outcomes.
questions.evidence: How we make a budget is just as important as the revenues and spending proposed within it.

questions.q: What must the US Congress pass if appropriations bills are not signed into law by 1 October?
questions.explain: It keeps the government funded temporarily.
questions.evidence: If the appropriations bills are not signed into law by Oct. 1 Congress must pass a continuing resolution

questions.q: Why is reconciliation a powerful budget tool in the US Senate?
options: They are written by the President
questions.explain: Under Senate rules they avoid unlimited debate.
questions.evidence: Reconciliation is a powerful tool because by Senate rules, reconciliation bills are not subject to filibuster.

questions.q: What is a filibuster?
options: A senator blocking a bill through unlimited debate
questions.explain: It exploits Senate rules that allow unlimited debate.
questions.evidence: taking advantage of Senate rules that allow for unlimited debate

questions.q: In incremental budgeting, what is the focal point of each year's budget?
options: A small increase or decrease over last year's budget
questions.explain: Incrementalism is simple but can lock in past decisions.
questions.evidence: the focal point for each year’s budget is an incremental increase or decrease over last year’s budget

questions.q: What criticism is made of 'balanced budgets' in state and local government?
questions.explain: One-time revenues can make a budget look balanced when it isn't.
questions.evidence: might actually hide structural deficits

questions.q: What is cost accounting (managerial accounting)?
options: Creating information about costs to inform management decisions
questions.explain: It supports pricing, budgeting and programme decisions.
questions.evidence: is the process of creating information about costs to inform management decisions

questions.q: Which question can cost analysis help managers answer?
options: What colour should the office be?
Will a new grant's revenue cover the cost of expanding a programme?
questions.explain: It also helps budget for new staff and assess economies of scale.
questions.evidence: Will the revenue from a new grant opportunity cover the costs to expand a program?

questions.q: In full cost accounting, what is the cost object?
options: The product or deliverable whose costs are measured
questions.explain: Defining it is the first of the six steps.
questions.evidence: The cost object is the product or deliverable for which costs are measured.

questions.q: What are direct costs often called?
questions.explain: They belong entirely to one cost centre, like its own staff salaries.
questions.evidence: often called “traceable costs

questions.q: What are most public organisations' costs related to?
questions.explain: Personnel costs are not spread evenly across clients or cases.
questions.evidence: costs are related to personnel, and personnel costs are not distributed evenly across clients or cases

questions.q: Why measure indirect costs even though they are hard to measure?
options: Because they are always the largest cost
To account properly for an activity's full cost
questions.explain: Ignoring indirect costs understates what services really cost.
questions.evidence: critically important to measure and properly account for full costs
